difficultyReason: Single-move argument using an analogy. The physician draws a parallel between two medical scenarios. Only one answer choice correctly names the analogical reasoning; other choices describe techniques the argument does not employ.
stimulus: Physician: When a patient has a bacterial infection and we prescribe antibiotics, we expect the infection to clear within days. Similarly, when a patient develops an autoimmune condition, we should expect that targeted immunosuppressants will resolve the condition quickly. The logic is the same: a targeted intervention addresses the root cause.
questionStem: The physician's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues from a sample of medical cases to a generalization about all patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites an authority in medicine to support a claim about treatment outcomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws an analogy between two medical scenarios to support a conclusion about one of them

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because one treatment works, a different treatment will work for another condition

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a prediction on a statistical comparison of disease outcomes

explanations.correct: The physician compares the bacterial-infection case (where antibiotics work quickly) to the autoimmune-condition case and applies the same logic. That is analogical reasoning: drawing a parallel to support a claim about one case using evidence about another.
explanations.A: The argument does not move from several cases to a general rule about all patients; it compares two specific types of cases.
explanations.B: No medical authority is cited; the physician reasons about the logic of the interventions.
explanations.D: This slightly mischaracterizes the analogy. The physician argues the treatments are similar in structure, not just that different treatments will work.
explanations.E: No statistical data about disease outcomes is presented.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a definition. The ethicist relies on a stated definition of 'theft' to classify an action. Only one answer describes this definitional application; others describe unrelated techniques.
stimulus: Ethicist: Theft is the unauthorized taking of another's property with intent to deprive that person of it. An employee who takes office supplies home without permission is committing theft under this definition, regardless of the minimal value of the items.

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a definition to determine whether a particular action falls under a given category

choices.label: B
choices.text: citing a counterexample to show that a general rule does not always apply

choices.label: C
choices.text: reasoning from the harmlessness of an action to the conclusion that it is not unethical

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from one workplace norm to a universal principle

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring the intent of an agent from the consequences of the agent's action

explanations.correct: The ethicist states a definition of theft and applies it to the case of office supplies, determining that the employee's action meets the definition's criteria. This is definitional application.
explanations.B: No counterexample is offered; the argument supports a position rather than attacking one.
explanations.C: The ethicist does not argue from harmlessness; instead, the minimal value is irrelevant to meeting the definition.
explanations.D: No workplace norm is generalized; the argument applies a stated definition.
explanations.E: The ethicist takes intent as a given element of the definition, not inferred from consequences.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument using a counterexample to refute a universal claim. The linguist provides a single case that contradicts the claim. Only one answer correctly names the counterexample technique; others describe irrelevant moves.
stimulus: Linguist: Some have claimed that all languages must have a word for the color red. However, the Pirahã language of the Amazon basin famously has no single term for red; speakers instead use phrases that reference the brightness of fire or blood. This counterexample shows the claim is false.
questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from a single linguistic example to a broad principle

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites a counterexample to a universal claim to show the claim is not always true

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a language is deficient because it lacks a common word

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers the structure of a language from the structure of its speakers' natural environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: appeals to the authority of linguistic experts to support a conclusion

explanations.correct: The linguist directly cites Pirahã as a case that violates the universal claim ('all languages must have a word for red'). This is textbook counterexample reasoning: one true instance that falsifies a universal statement.
explanations.A: The argument works in the opposite direction: it uses a specific example to refute a general claim, not to support one.
explanations.C: The linguist does not evaluate the Pirahã language as deficient; the existence of an alternative expression is the point.
explanations.D: No inference about language structure from environment is made.
explanations.E: No appeal to expert authority; the linguist reasons from a publicly acknowledged fact about Pirahã.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a general principle to a specific case. The economist states a principle about inflation and applies it to a particular economy. Only one answer correctly describes this application; others describe unrelated techniques.
stimulus: Economist: Whenever a central bank rapidly increases the money supply without a corresponding increase in goods and services, inflation results. The Central Reserve increased the money supply by 8 percent last year while gross domestic product grew only 2 percent. Therefore, we should expect significant inflation in the coming months.
questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites a historical precedent to predict a future economic outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a general economic principle to a particular situation to support a specific prediction

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from a correlation between two economic variables

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the economic policies of one nation to the policies of all nations

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that rapid money supply growth will always cause inflation without exception

explanations.correct: The economist first states a general principle (rapid money-supply increases without corresponding output growth cause inflation), then applies it to a concrete case (the Central Reserve's recent actions), concluding inflation will result. That is principle-to-case application.
explanations.A: No historical precedent is cited; the argument uses a general principle.
explanations.C: The argument does not infer causation from observed correlation; it applies an already-established principle.
explanations.D: No generalization across nations is made; the principle applies universally but the application is to one specific case.
explanations.E: The principle allows for some exceptions in principle; the argument claims the condition is met in this case.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument citing expert authority. The environmental scientist appeals to expert consensus to support a conclusion. Only one answer correctly names the appeal-to-authority technique; others describe unrelated moves.
stimulus: Environmental scientist: The overwhelming consensus among climate scientists worldwide is that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions are driving rapid global warming. Given the expertise and rigor of the scientific consensus, we should adjust our environmental policies accordingly.

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites the consensus of expert opinion to support a claim about environmental policy

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from climate patterns in one region to predictions about global climate

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a policy will succeed because it aligns with majority opinion

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal mechanism from observations of statistical correlation

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects a competing theory by showing it contradicts established scientific law

explanations.correct: The scientist explicitly cites the consensus view of climate experts as a basis for accepting the claim about anthropogenic warming and making policy recommendations. This is a direct appeal to expert authority.
explanations.B: No regional data or generalization to global climate is presented; the argument cites scientific consensus.
explanations.C: Majority opinion is not invoked; the argument appeals to expert consensus specifically.
explanations.D: No causal inference from correlation is drawn; the consensus is treated as authoritative.
explanations.E: No competing theory is explicitly rejected; the argument appeals to the positive consensus view.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument drawing an analogy between a hypothetical case and a real policy. The policy analyst compares two governance structures. Only one answer correctly names analogical reasoning; others describe unrelated techniques.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Allowing corporations to self-regulate environmental standards is like hiring a student to grade their own exam. In both cases, the evaluator has a direct incentive to report a favorable outcome, undermining the integrity of the assessment. Therefore, corporations cannot be trusted to enforce their own environmental standards.
questionStem: The analyst's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: argues from a generalization about academic practices to a conclusion about corporate behavior

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses an analogy to suggest that a policy is flawed because a parallel situation is obviously problematic

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites empirical evidence that corporations have failed to regulate themselves

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal mechanism that explains corporate noncompliance with standards

choices.label: E
choices.text: applies a principle about conflicts of interest to the specific case of corporate regulation

explanations.correct: The analyst draws a parallel between self-grading (clearly problematic) and self-regulation (the policy in question). The analogy illustrates why the policy is flawed: both involve conflicted evaluators with incentives to report favorably.
explanations.A: This is an analogy, not a generalization from academic practices to corporate behavior per se.
explanations.C: No empirical evidence of past corporate failures is cited.
explanations.D: The causal mechanism (incentive misalignment) is explained through the analogy, not inferred independently.
explanations.E: While a principle about conflicts of interest is implicit, the reasoning is fundamentally analogical, not principle-based.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument using a counterexample. The historian provides a historical case that contradicts a claim about law. Only one answer correctly names the counterexample technique; others describe unrelated reasoning moves.
stimulus: Historian: It is sometimes claimed that common law systems always protect individual rights more effectively than civil law systems. However, several civil law countries, including Portugal and Spain, have robust constitutional protections for individual freedoms. This shows the claim is too broad.
questionStem: Which one of the following describes a technique of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from two civil law systems to a conclusion about all civil law systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: cites concrete historical examples to refute a universal claim about legal systems

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that civil law is superior to common law based on a comparison of protections

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because two countries share a legal tradition, they have identical rights protections

choices.label: E
choices.text: applies a principle from constitutional theory to evaluate competing legal systems

explanations.correct: The historian provides concrete historical examples (Portugal and Spain) that contradict the universal claim that common law always protects rights more effectively. These are counterexamples: specific instances that show the claim is false.
explanations.A: While two examples are cited, the reasoning is not a generalization; it is a refutation of a universal claim using counterexamples.
explanations.C: The argument does not establish civil law superiority; it only shows the original claim is too broad.
explanations.D: No such inference is made; the examples are cited to refute a claim, not to compare countries within a tradition.
explanations.E: No abstract principle is applied; the argument relies on historical facts.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument applying a definition to resolve a dispute. The lawyer uses a legal definition to classify a contract term. Only one answer correctly describes definitional application; others describe unrelated techniques.
stimulus: Lawyer: A contract is unconscionable if one party had no meaningful choice and the terms unreasonably favor the other party. This employment contract requires workers to waive all legal claims in exchange for continued employment, and most workers have no realistic alternative employment. Therefore, the contract is unconscionable under the legal definition.
questionStem: The lawyer's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: establishes a causal link between a contractual term and economic harm

choices.label: B
choices.text: applies a legal definition to determine whether a contract meets the criteria for a particular classification

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites precedent from prior cases to support a conclusion about the current contract

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that the workers would have rejected the contract if they had been fully informed

choices.label: E
choices.text: infers the intent of the employer from the restrictive language of the contract

explanations.correct: The lawyer states the legal definition of unconscionability and applies it point by point to the contract: lack of meaningful choice (workers have no alternatives) and unreasonably favorable terms (broad waiver of legal claims). This is definitional application to determine classification.
explanations.A: The argument does not establish a causal mechanism; it applies a definition.
explanations.D: The argument does not counterfactually speculate about worker preferences; it applies a legal standard.
explanations.E: The employer's intent is not inferred; the definition focuses on the situation and terms, not intent.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument using an analogy between two technological systems. The engineer draws a parallel to support a design claim. Only one answer correctly names analogical reasoning; others describe unrelated techniques.
stimulus: Engineer: The redundancy in airplane engine design has proven invaluable for safety: if one engine fails, the aircraft can still reach its destination. Similarly, data storage systems with redundant backups protect against catastrophic loss. Therefore, critical software systems should be designed with redundant components.
questionStem: The engineer's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: generalizes from the success of redundancy in aviation to the success of redundancy in all systems

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws an analogy between two systems with redundant design to support a recommendation for a third

choices.label: C
choices.text: cites statistical evidence that redundancy improves system reliability

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers that because two technologies are similar in one respect, they are similar in all respects

choices.label: E
choices.text: argues that redundant systems are always more expensive but worth the cost

explanations.correct: The engineer compares airplane engines (redundancy works for safety) and data storage (redundancy prevents loss) to support a conclusion about software systems. This is analogical reasoning: using parallel cases to support a recommendation.
explanations.A: The analogy is limited to two successful examples; it does not overgeneralize to all systems.
explanations.D: The argument identifies a specific parallel (redundancy benefit), not a claim of similarity in all respects.
explanations.E: Cost is not addressed; the argument focuses on the benefit of redundancy.

difficultyReason: Single-move argument citing expert opinion. The music critic appeals to the judgment of experienced musicians. Only one answer correctly names the appeal-to-authority technique; others describe unrelated reasoning moves.
stimulus: Music critic: Professional conductors and orchestral musicians consistently regard the symphonies of Mahler as among the most challenging to perform well. Given the expertise of these musicians, their assessment should inform our understanding of Mahler's compositional complexity. Therefore, Mahler's work demonstrates extraordinary technical mastery.

choices.label: A
choices.text: cites the judgment of experienced practitioners to support a claim about artistic achievement

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the difficulty of Mahler's work to a universal principle about musical complexity

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers that if musicians find a work difficult, the composer intended it to be difficult

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that a work is great because performers struggle with it

choices.label: E
choices.text: draws an analogy between Mahler's symphonies and other challenging musical compositions

explanations.correct: The critic appeals to the consistent judgment of professional musicians (conductors and orchestral musicians) as evidence supporting the claim about Mahler's technical mastery. This is an appeal to expert authority.
explanations.B: The argument cites expert judgment, not a generalization from specific cases to a universal rule.
explanations.C: No inference about the composer's intentions is made.
explanations.D: The argument does not equate difficulty with greatness; it uses difficulty as evidence of mastery.
explanations.E: No analogy to other compositions is drawn; the argument cites expert consensus about Mahler alone.
